stem: Calculate the mole fraction of ethylene glycol \(\text{(C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2)\) in a solution containing 20% of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2\) by mass.
solution:
Assume that we have \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution (one can start with any amount of solution because the results obtained will be the same). Solution will contain \(20\,\text{g}\) of ethylene glycol and \(80\,\text{g}\) of water.

Molar mass of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 = 12 \times 2 + 1 \times 6 + 16 \times 2 = 62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

Moles of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{20\,\text{g}}{62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.322\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of water \(= \dfrac{80\,\text{g}}{18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 4.444\,\text{mol}\)

\(x_{\text{glycol}} = \dfrac{\text{moles of }\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2}{\text{moles of }\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 + \text{moles of }\text{H}_2\text{O}} = \dfrac{0.322\,\text{mol}}{0.322\,\text{mol} + 4.444\,\text{mol}} = 0.068\)

Similarly, \(x_{\text{water}} = \dfrac{4.444\,\text{mol}}{0.322\,\text{mol} + 4.444\,\text{mol}} = 0.932\)

Mole fraction of water can also be calculated as: \(1 - 0.068 = 0.932\)

stem: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing \(5\,\text{g}\) of NaOH in \(450\,\text{mL}\) solution.
solution:
Moles of NaOH \(= \dfrac{5\,\text{g}}{40\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.125\,\text{mol}\)

Volume of the solution in litres \(= 450\,\text{mL} / 1000\,\text{mL L}^{-1}\)

Using equation (2.8),

Molarity \(= \dfrac{0.125\,\text{mol} \times 1000\,\text{mL L}^{-1}}{450\,\text{mL}} = 0.278\,\text{M}\)

\(= 0.278\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

\(= 0.278\,\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
_note: The book's printed solution cites "equation (2.8)"; the molarity definition in this chapter is equation (1.8). Stale cross-reference left over from an edition in which this was Unit 2. Transcribed faithfully, not corrected.

stem: Calculate molality of \(2.5\,\text{g}\) of ethanoic acid \((\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})\) in \(75\,\text{g}\) of benzene.
solution:
Molar mass of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2\): \(12 \times 2 + 1 \times 4 + 16 \times 2 = 60\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{2.5\,\text{g}}{60\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.0417\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of benzene in kg \(= 75\,\text{g}/1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1} = 75 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}\)

Molality of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{\text{Moles of }\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2}{\text{kg of benzene}} = \dfrac{0.0417\,\text{mol} \times 1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}}{75\,\text{g}}\)

\(= 0.556\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

stem: If \(\text{N}_2\) gas is bubbled through water at \(293\,\text{K}\), how many millimoles of \(\text{N}_2\) gas would dissolve in 1 litre of water? Assume that \(\text{N}_2\) exerts a partial pressure of \(0.987\,\text{bar}\). Given that Henry's law constant for \(\text{N}_2\) at \(293\,\text{K}\) is \(76.48\,k\text{bar}\).
solution:
The solubility of gas is related to the mole fraction in aqueous solution. The mole fraction of the gas in the solution is calculated by applying Henry's law. Thus:

\(x\,(\text{Nitrogen}) = \dfrac{p\,(\text{nitrogen})}{K_{\text{H}}} = \dfrac{0.987\,\text{bar}}{76{,}480\,\text{bar}} = 1.29 \times 10^{-5}\)

As 1 litre of water contains \(55.5\,\text{mol}\) of it, therefore if \(n\) represents number of moles of \(\text{N}_2\) in solution,

\(x\,(\text{Nitrogen}) = \dfrac{n\,\text{mol}}{n\,\text{mol} + 55.5\,\text{mol}} = \dfrac{n}{55.5} = 1.29 \times 10^{-5}\)

(\(n\) in denominator is neglected as it is \(<< 55.5\))

Thus \(n = 1.29 \times 10^{-5} \times 55.5\,\text{mol} = 7.16 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}\)

\(= \dfrac{7.16 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol} \times 1000\,\text{mmol}}{1\,\text{mol}} = 0.716\,\text{mmol}\)

stem: Vapour pressure of chloroform \((\text{CHCl}_3)\) and dichloromethane \((\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2)\) at \(298\,\text{K}\) are \(200\,\text{mm Hg}\) and \(415\,\text{mm Hg}\) respectively. (i) Calculate the vapour pressure of the solution prepared by mixing \(25.5\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CHCl}_3\) and \(40\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\) at \(298\,\text{K}\) and, (ii) mole fractions of each component in vapour phase.
solution:
(i) Molar mass of \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2 = 12 \times 1 + 1 \times 2 + 35.5 \times 2 = 85\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Molar mass of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = 12 \times 1 + 1 \times 1 + 35.5 \times 3 = 119.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2 = \dfrac{40\,\text{g}}{85\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.47\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = \dfrac{25.5\,\text{g}}{119.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.213\,\text{mol}\)

Total number of moles \(= 0.47 + 0.213 = 0.683\,\text{mol}\)

\(x_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = \dfrac{0.47\,\text{mol}}{0.683\,\text{mol}} = 0.688\)

\(x_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 1.00 - 0.688 = 0.312\)

Using equation (2.16),

\(p_{\text{total}} = p_1^0 + (p_2^0 - p_1^0)\,x_2 = 200 + (415 - 200) \times 0.688\)

\(= 200 + 147.9 = 347.9\,\text{mm Hg}\)

(ii) Using the relation (2.19), \(y_{\text{i}} = p_{\text{i}}/p_{\text{total}}\), we can calculate the mole fraction of the components in gas phase \((y_{\text{i}})\).

\(p_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = 0.688 \times 415\,\text{mm Hg} = 285.5\,\text{mm Hg}\)

\(p_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 0.312 \times 200\,\text{mm Hg} = 62.4\,\text{mm Hg}\)

\(y_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = 285.5\,\text{mm Hg}/347.9\,\text{mm Hg} = 0.82\)

\(y_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 62.4\,\text{mm Hg}/347.9\,\text{mm Hg} = 0.18\)

**Note:** Since \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\) is a more volatile component than \(\text{CHCl}_3\), \([\,p^0_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = 415\,\text{mm Hg}\) and \(p^0_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 200\,\text{mm Hg}]\) and the vapour phase is also richer in \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\) \([\,y_{\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2} = 0.82\) and \(y_{\text{CHCl}_3} = 0.18]\), it may thus be concluded that at equilibrium, vapour phase will be always rich in the component which is more volatile.
_note: The book's printed solution cites "equation (2.16)" and "relation (2.19)"; in this chapter these are equations (1.16) and (1.19). Stale cross-references left over from an edition in which this was Unit 2 (the same slip as Eg 1.2). Transcribed faithfully, not corrected.

stem: The vapour pressure of pure benzene at a certain temperature is \(0.850\,\text{bar}\). A non-volatile, non-electrolyte solid weighing \(0.5\,\text{g}\) when added to \(39.0\,\text{g}\) of benzene (molar mass \(78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)). Vapour pressure of the solution, then, is \(0.845\,\text{bar}\). What is the molar mass of the solid substance?
solution:
The various quantities known to us are as follows:

\(p_1^{0} = 0.850\,\text{bar}\); \(p = 0.845\,\text{bar}\); \(M_1 = 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(w_2 = 0.5\,\text{g}\); \(w_1 = 39\,\text{g}\)

Substituting these values in equation (2.28), we get

\(\dfrac{0.850\,\text{bar} - 0.845\,\text{bar}}{0.850\,\text{bar}} = \dfrac{0.5\,\text{g} \times 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{M_2 \times 39\,\text{g}}\)

Therefore, \(M_2 = 170\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The book's printed solution cites "equation (2.28)"; the equation it substitutes into is (1.28) on the preceding page. Stale cross-reference from an earlier edition in which this was Chapter 2. Transcribed as printed.

stem: \(18\,\text{g}\) of glucose, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\), is dissolved in \(1\,\text{kg}\) of water in a saucepan. At what temperature will water boil at \(1.013\,\text{bar}\)? \(K_b\) for water is \(0.52\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\).
solution:
Moles of glucose \(= 18\,\text{g} / 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1} = 0.1\,\text{mol}\)

Number of kilograms of solvent \(= 1\,\text{kg}\)

Thus molality of glucose solution \(= 0.1\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

For water, change in boiling point

\(\Delta T_b = K_b \times m = 0.52\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 0.1\,\text{mol kg}^{-1} = 0.052\,\text{K}\)

Since water boils at \(373.15\,\text{K}\) at \(1.013\,\text{bar}\) pressure, therefore, the boiling point of solution will be \(373.15 + 0.052 = 373.202\,\text{K}\).

stem: The boiling point of benzene is \(353.23\,\text{K}\). When \(1.80\,\text{g}\) of a non-volatile solute was dissolved in \(90\,\text{g}\) of benzene, the boiling point is raised to \(354.11\,\text{K}\). Calculate the molar mass of the solute. \(K_b\) for benzene is \(2.53\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\).
solution:
The elevation \((\Delta T_b)\) in the boiling point \(= 354.11\,\text{K} - 353.23\,\text{K} = 0.88\,\text{K}\)

Substituting these values in expression (2.33) we get

\(M_2 = \dfrac{2.53\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 1.8\,\text{g} \times 1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}}{0.88\,\text{K} \times 90\,\text{g}} = 58\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Therefore, molar mass of the solute, \(M_2 = 58\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The book's printed solution cites "expression (2.33)"; the equation used is (1.33) on the preceding page — the same stale Chapter-2 cross-reference as Eg 1.6. The page also prints the subtraction as "353. 23 K" with a stray space after the decimal point; transcribed as 353.23 K.

stem: \(45\,\text{g}\) of ethylene glycol \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2)\) is mixed with \(600\,\text{g}\) of water. Calculate (a) the freezing point depression and (b) the freezing point of the solution.
solution:
Depression in freezing point is related to the molality, therefore, the molality of the solution with respect to ethylene glycol \(= \dfrac{\text{moles of ethylene glycol}}{\text{mass of water in kilogram}}\)

Moles of ethylene glycol \(= \dfrac{45\,\text{g}}{62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.73\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of water in kg \(= \dfrac{600\,\text{g}}{1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}} = 0.6\,\text{kg}\)

Hence molality of ethylene glycol \(= \dfrac{0.73\,\text{mol}}{0.60\,\text{kg}} = 1.2\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

Therefore freezing point depression,

\(\Delta T_f = 1.86\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 1.2\,\text{mol kg}^{-1} = 2.2\,\text{K}\)

Freezing point of the aqueous solution \(= 273.15\,\text{K} - 2.2\,\text{K} = 270.95\,\text{K}\)
_note: Font-substitution artifact on the printed page: the delta in the freezing-point-depression line is set as a Latin "Ä" (it reads "ÄT_f = 1.86 K kg mol^-1 ..."). Every other occurrence in the chapter is a proper Δ, so this is a typesetting fault, not a different symbol; transcribed as \Delta T_f.

stem: \(1.00\,\text{g}\) of a non-electrolyte solute dissolved in \(50\,\text{g}\) of benzene lowered the freezing point of benzene by \(0.40\,\text{K}\). The freezing point depression constant of benzene is \(5.12\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\). Find the molar mass of the solute.
solution:
Substituting the values of various terms involved in equation (1.36) we get,

\(M_2 = \dfrac{5.12\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 1.00\,\text{g} \times 1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}}{0.40 \times 50\,\text{g}} = 256\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Thus, molar mass of the solute \(= 256\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The printed denominator is "0.40 × 50 g" — the unit K is dropped from the 0.40 (it is ΔT_f = 0.40 K). Transcribed as printed; the numerical result 256 g mol^-1 is unaffected.

stem: \(200\,\text{cm}^3\) of an aqueous solution of a protein contains \(1.26\,\text{g}\) of the protein. The osmotic pressure of such a solution at \(300\,\text{K}\) is found to be \(2.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar}\). Calculate the molar mass of the protein.
solution:
The various quantities known to us are as follows: \(\Pi = 2.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar}\),

\(V = 200\,\text{cm}^3 = 0.200\,\text{litre}\)

\(T = 300\,\text{K}\)

\(R = 0.083\,\text{L bar mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\)

Substituting these values in equation (2.42) we get

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1.26\,\text{g} \times 0.083\,\text{L bar K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1} \times 300\,\text{K}}{2.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar} \times 0.200\,\text{L}} = 61{,}022\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The book's printed solution cites "equation (2.42)"; the equation used is (1.42) on the preceding page — the third instance in this band of the stale Chapter-2 cross-reference (see also Eg 1.6 and Eg 1.8).

stem: Calculate the osmotic pressure in pascals exerted by a solution prepared by dissolving \(1.0\,\text{g}\) of polymer of molar mass \(185{,}000\) in \(450\,\text{mL}\) of water at \(37\,^\circ\text{C}\).

\(2\,\text{g}\) of benzoic acid \((\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH})\) dissolved in \(25\,\text{g}\) of benzene shows a depression in freezing point equal to \(1.62\,\text{K}\). Molal depression constant for benzene is \(4.9\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\). What is the percentage association of acid if it forms dimer in solution?
solution:
The given quantities are: \(w_2 = 2\,\text{g}\); \(K_f = 4.9\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\); \(w_1 = 25\,\text{g}\), \(\Delta T_f = 1.62\,\text{K}\)

Substituting these values in equation (1.36) we get:

\(M_2 = \dfrac{4.9\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 2\,\text{g} \times 1000\,\text{g kg}^{-1}}{25\,\text{g} \times 1.62\,\text{K}} = 241.98\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Thus, experimental molar mass of benzoic acid in benzene is \(= 241.98\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Now consider the following equilibrium for the acid:

\(2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons (\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH})_2\)

If \(x\) represents the degree of association of the solute then we would have \((1 - x)\) mol of benzoic acid left in unassociated form and correspondingly \(\dfrac{x}{2}\) as associated moles of benzoic acid at equilibrium. Therefore, total number of moles of particles at equilibrium is:

\(1 - x + \dfrac{x}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{x}{2}\)

Thus, total number of moles of particles at equilibrium equals van't Hoff factor \(i\).

But \(i = \dfrac{\text{Normal molar mass}}{\text{Abnormal molar mass}} = \dfrac{122\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{241.98\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}\)

or \(\dfrac{x}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{122}{241.98} = 1 - 0.504 = 0.496\)

or \(x = 2 \times 0.496 = 0.992\)

Therefore, degree of association of benzoic acid in benzene is \(99.2\,\%\).

stem: \(0.6\,\text{mL}\) of acetic acid \((\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})\), having density \(1.06\,\text{g mL}^{-1}\), is dissolved in \(1\,\text{litre}\) of water. The depression in freezing point observed for this strength of acid was \(0.0205\,^\circ\text{C}\). Calculate the van't Hoff factor and the dissociation constant of acid.
solution:
Number of moles of acetic acid \(= \dfrac{0.6\,\text{mL} \times 1.06\,\text{g mL}^{-1}}{60\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.0106\,\text{mol} = n\)

Molality \(= \dfrac{0.0106\,\text{mol}}{1000\,\text{mL} \times 1\,\text{g mL}^{-1}} = 0.0106\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

Using equation (1.35)

\(\Delta T_f = 1.86\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1} \times 0.0106\,\text{mol kg}^{-1} = 0.0197\,\text{K}\)

van't Hoff Factor \((i) = \dfrac{\text{Observed freezing point}}{\text{Calculated freezing point}} = \dfrac{0.0205\,\text{K}}{0.0197\,\text{K}} = 1.041\)

Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte and will dissociate into two ions: acetate and hydrogen ions per molecule of acetic acid. If \(x\) is the degree of dissociation of acetic acid, then we would have \(n(1 - x)\) moles of undissociated acetic acid, \(nx\) moles of \(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-\) and \(nx\) moles of \(\text{H}^+\) ions,

\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-\)

\(n\) mol, \(0\), \(0\)

\(n(1 - x)\), \(nx\) mol, \(nx\) mol

Thus total moles of particles are: \(n(1 - x + x + x) = n(1 + x)\)

\(i = \dfrac{n(1 + x)}{n} = 1 + x = 1.041\)

Thus degree of dissociation of acetic acid \(= x = 1.041 - 1.000 = 0.041\)

Then \([\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}] = n(1 - x) = 0.0106\,(1 - 0.041)\),

\([\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-] = nx = 0.0106 \times 0.041\), \([\text{H}^+] = nx = 0.0106 \times 0.041\).

\(K_a = \dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-][\text{H}^+]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]} = \dfrac{0.0106 \times 0.041 \times 0.0106 \times 0.041}{0.0106\,(1.00 - 0.041)} = 1.86 \times 10^{-5}\)
_note: The observed depression is stated as 0.0205 °C in the stem and then used as 0.0205 K in the van't Hoff ratio; the two are equal as a temperature DIFFERENCE, so the arithmetic is sound. Transcribed as printed.

stem: At \(300\,\text{K}\), \(36\,\text{g}\) of glucose present in a litre of its solution has an osmotic pressure of \(4.98\,\text{bar}\). If the osmotic pressure of the solution is \(1.52\,\text{bar}\) at the same temperature, what would be its concentration?

Suggest the most important type of intermolecular attractive interaction in the following pairs.
(i) n-hexane and n-octane
(ii) \(\text{I}_2\) and \(\text{CCl}_4\)
(iii) \(\text{NaClO}_4\) and water
(iv) methanol and acetone
(v) acetonitrile \((\text{CH}_3\text{CN})\) and acetone \((\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O})\).
Based on solute-solvent interactions, arrange the following in order of increasing solubility in n-octane and explain. Cyclohexane, \(\text{KCl}\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CN}\).

Amongst the following compounds, identify which are insoluble, partially soluble and highly soluble in water?
(i) phenol
(ii) toluene
(iii) formic acid
(iv) ethylene glycol
(v) chloroform
(vi) pentanol.
If the density of some lake water is \(1.25\,\text{g mL}^{-1}\) and contains \(92\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{Na}^+\) ions per kg of water, calculate the molarity of \(\text{Na}^+\) ions in the lake.
If the solubility product of \(\text{CuS}\) is \(6 \times 10^{-16}\), calculate the maximum molarity of \(\text{CuS}\) in aqueous solution.

Calculate the mass percentage of aspirin \((\text{C}_9\text{H}_8\text{O}_4)\) in acetonitrile \((\text{CH}_3\text{CN})\) when \(6.5\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{C}_9\text{H}_8\text{O}_4\) is dissolved in \(450\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CH}_3\text{CN}\).

Nalorphene \((\text{C}_{19}\text{H}_{21}\text{NO}_3)\), similar to morphine, is used to combat withdrawal symptoms in narcotic users. Dose of nalorphene generally given is \(1.5\,\text{mg}\). Calculate the mass of \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\) aqueous solution required for the above dose.
Calculate the amount of benzoic acid \((\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH})\) required for preparing \(250\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.15\,\text{M}\) solution in methanol.
The depression in freezing point of water observed for the same amount of acetic acid, trichloroacetic acid and trifluoroacetic acid increases in the order given above. Explain briefly.

Calculate the depression in the freezing point of water when \(10\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHClCOOH}\) is added to \(250\,\text{g}\) of water. \(K_a = 1.4 \times 10^{-3}\), \(K_f = 1.86\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\).

\(19.5\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CH}_2\text{FCOOH}\) is dissolved in \(500\,\text{g}\) of water. The depression in the freezing point of water observed is \(1.0^\circ\text{C}\). Calculate the van't Hoff factor and dissociation constant of fluoroacetic acid.
_note: The book sets the degree sign as a superscript zero: it prints "1.0\(^0\) C". Transcribed as \(1.0^\circ\text{C}\); the meaning is unambiguous.

stem: Vapour pressure of water at \(293\,\text{K}\) is \(17.535\,\text{mm Hg}\). Calculate the vapour pressure of water at \(293\,\text{K}\) when \(25\,\text{g}\) of glucose is dissolved in \(450\,\text{g}\) of water.

Henry's law constant for the molality of methane in benzene at \(298\,\text{K}\) is \(4.27 \times 10^5\,\text{mm Hg}\). Calculate the solubility of methane in benzene at \(298\,\text{K}\) under \(760\,\text{mm Hg}\).

\(100\,\text{g}\) of liquid A (molar mass \(140\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)) was dissolved in \(1000\,\text{g}\) of liquid B (molar mass \(180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)). The vapour pressure of pure liquid B was found to be \(500\,\text{torr}\). Calculate the vapour pressure of pure liquid A and its vapour pressure in the solution if the total vapour pressure of the solution is \(475\,\text{Torr}\).

Vapour pressures of pure acetone and chloroform at \(328\,\text{K}\) are \(741.8\,\text{mm Hg}\) and \(632.8\,\text{mm Hg}\) respectively. Assuming that they form ideal solution over the entire range of composition, plot \(p_{\text{total}}\), \(p_{\text{chloroform}}\), and \(p_{\text{acetone}}\) as a function of \(x_{\text{acetone}}\). The experimental data observed for different compositions of mixture is:

| \(100 \times x_{\text{acetone}}\) | 0 | 11.8 | 23.4 | 36.0 | 50.8 | 58.2 | 64.5 | 72.1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(p_{\text{acetone}}\) /mm Hg | 0 | 54.9 | 110.1 | 202.4 | 322.7 | 405.9 | 454.1 | 521.1 |
| \(p_{\text{chloroform}}\) /mm Hg | 632.8 | 548.1 | 469.4 | 359.7 | 257.7 | 193.6 | 161.2 | 120.7 |

Plot this data also on the same graph paper. Indicate whether it has positive deviation or negative deviation from the ideal solution.

Benzene and toluene form ideal solution over the entire range of composition. The vapour pressure of pure benzene and toluene at \(300\,\text{K}\) are \(50.71\,\text{mm Hg}\) and \(32.06\,\text{mm Hg}\) respectively. Calculate the mole fraction of benzene in vapour phase if \(80\,\text{g}\) of benzene is mixed with \(100\,\text{g}\) of toluene.

The air is a mixture of a number of gases. The major components are oxygen and nitrogen with approximate proportion of 20% is to 79% by volume at \(298\,\text{K}\). The water is in equilibrium with air at a pressure of \(10\,\text{atm}\). At \(298\,\text{K}\) if the Henry's law constants for oxygen and nitrogen at \(298\,\text{K}\) are \(3.30 \times 10^7\,\text{mm}\) and \(6.51 \times 10^7\,\text{mm}\) respectively, calculate the composition of these gases in water.
_note: Printed as "20% is to 79%" — the book states the oxygen:nitrogen proportion as a ratio in that wording, and the two percentages sum to 99%, not 100%. Transcribed exactly as printed; not corrected.

stem: Determine the amount of \(\text{CaCl}_2\) \((i = 2.47)\) dissolved in \(2.5\,\text{litre}\) of water such that its osmotic pressure is \(0.75\,\text{atm}\) at \(27^\circ\text{C}\).

Determine the osmotic pressure of a solution prepared by dissolving \(25\,\text{mg}\) of \(\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4\) in \(2\,\text{litre}\) of water at \(25^\circ\text{C}\), assuming that it is completely dissociated.
